exit_trigger: Not applicable until a position exists; If research shows the moat is weak or must be rebuilt continuously, remove from the watch list; If the ten-year earnings record shows losses or a significant decline, reject; If leverage rises above a debt-to-equity of 0.5, reject
rationale: The numbers in front of me look like a good business: a 5-year average ROE of 30.6%, a market cap of about $7.35 billion, and a stated margin of safety of 38.5% against a DCF value of $1,271.73 a share. But a stock is a piece of a business, and this snapshot tells me nothing about the business itself: no ten-year earnings record, no description of the moat, no look at management, no cost-of-capital detail beyond the 5% discount rate. Debt-to-equity of 0.497 clears my 0.5 limit by a hair, with no room to spare. That DCF also leans on an 8% growth rate (trailing CAGR was 13.9%, capped) and a 5% discount rate, and owner earnings of about $413 million against a $7.35 billion market cap is a yield near 5.6%, which is not a wide cushion. I'm not buying on a spreadsheet alone. I'll keep this on the watch list until the moat and the earnings record are verified, and I'll happily pass if they don't hold up.

exit_trigger: Not applicable, since no position is taken; I would reconsider only on verifiable evidence of durable pricing power or a structural cost advantage, a documented 10-year earnings record, and a margin of safety of at least 15%
rationale: I understand this business: Best Buy sells other people's electronics at a thin spread, and the manufacturers and online rivals can sell the same box to the same customer. The numbers in front of me look decent. The snapshot shows a 17.7% margin of safety, a debt-to-equity of 0.39 and a 5-year average ROE of 48.4%. But a cheap price on a business without a durable moat is the cigar-butt trap I fell into with Berkshire's textile mill. I can't point to pricing power, a cost advantage I can verify, or customers who would resist switching, and I can't verify a 10-year earnings record from this snapshot. I'll pass, and I'm perfectly happy to sit in cash waiting for a better pitch.

rationale: I can explain this business in two paragraphs: it sells premium athletic apparel under its own brand. The numbers I was handed look wonderful: a 5-year average ROE of 34.6%, debt-to-equity of 0.0, and owner earnings of about $1.32 billion against a $12.1 billion market cap. But a 68% margin of safety from a DCF with an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate makes me suspicious of the model, not excited about the stock. Apparel is a fashion-driven business, and I cannot verify from this snapshot that the brand holds pricing power through a full cycle. I also have no 10-year earnings history and no management record, and I don't buy on the fields that happen to look good. I'll put it on the watch list and wait for the evidence.

exit_trigger: Not applicable - no position is recommended; Would revisit only if evidence emerged of a durable moat (pricing power, structural cost advantage) and a verified 10-year earnings record
rationale: I understand selling cars and trucks and servicing them; we have owned dealerships at Berkshire, so this is inside my circle. The numbers in front of me are respectable: a 5-year average ROE of about 23.8%, debt-to-equity of about 0.39, and a price roughly 18% below the stated intrinsic value. But a good return on equity is not a moat. A dealer buys a product made by someone else, sells it in a competitive local market, and rides a cyclical business that the manufacturers and a changing retail model could reshape. I can't point to pricing power that lasts 10 years, and the snapshot doesn't show me a 10-year earnings record or the CEO's tenure either. A fair business at a decent price is not what I'm hunting for, so I pass.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand pricing power eroding, such as sustained price cuts or share loss to private label; Management making value-destroying acquisitions or overpaying for buybacks; Discovery that the reported debt-to-equity of 0.10 materially understates leverage; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value with a persistent gap
rationale: Packaged food with household brands is a business I can explain in two paragraphs, and it sits inside my circle. On the numbers I was handed, this looks cheap: $21.93 against an intrinsic value of $43.71, a 49.8% margin of safety, with five-year average owner earnings of about $829 million against a market cap of about $6.5 billion. But the model assumes zero growth, and the snapshot is silent on ten years of earnings history, CEO tenure, ROIC, and the Treasury yield. A debt-to-equity of 0.10 also sounds too good for a mature food company, and I can't verify what is behind it. A cheap price on a mature brand portfolio is not enough. Until I can confirm the earnings record and the debt picture, I'll watch rather than buy.

exit_trigger: Evidence that gross margins or pricing power are eroding against large or online competitors; Capital allocation that destroys value, such as expensive acquisitions or buybacks well above intrinsic value; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; Debt-to-equity rising materially above 0.5
rationale: MSM sells industrial supplies to manufacturers, a business I can explain simply. The numbers I was given look good: a 5-year average ROE of 20.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.35, and a 21.9% margin of safety against an intrinsic value of $157.18. But the snapshot gives me no evidence of a moat, no 10-year earnings record, and nothing on management, and I won't buy a distributor on a hunch. The valuation also rests on 8% growth (a 9.0% trailing CAGR, capped) and a 5% discount rate, and owner earnings of $302.96 million on a $6.85 billion market cap is only about a 4.4% yield. Until I can verify that this distributor has pricing power or real customer stickiness rather than just good recent returns, I keep my cash and wait.

exit_trigger: Evidence of erosion in pricing power or market share in core water heating; Management making value-destroying acquisitions or abandoning balance sheet discipline; Price exceeding 1.5x a conservatively re-estimated intrinsic value
rationale: A.O. Smith makes water heaters and water treatment products, a business I can describe in two paragraphs, and the snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 23.7% with debt-to-equity of 0.083. At $64.85 against a computed intrinsic value of $95.72, the stated margin of safety is 32.3%, well above my 15% bar, though that value rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate that I would want to haircut. What I cannot verify from this snapshot is the ten years of positive earnings, the CEO's tenure and record, and any hard evidence of pricing power or share trends. Without those, I don't have a moat I can put a number on, only a reasonable impression of one. I'd rather wait and do the homework than buy a wonderful price on a business I haven't fully checked.

exit_trigger: Evidence of eroding pricing power or brand strength (volume loss after price increases); Debt turns out to be materially higher than the reported ratio suggests and is used to fund overpriced acquisitions; Management dishonesty or value-destroying capital allocation; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value with a persistent gap
rationale: This is a coatings and sealants maker that sells products people buy over and over, and I can explain it in two paragraphs, so it sits inside my circle. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 22.9% and an estimated margin of safety of 20.1% against my 15% bar, which is encouraging. But I won't buy on the fields that happen to be present. The filing gives me no 10-year earnings record, no CEO tenure, and no insider or 13F data. The debt-to-equity of 0.0027 looks too small to take at face value, and I'd want to see the debt itself before believing it. The intrinsic value also rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and the owner-earnings yield is only about 4.3% of market cap, so I'd rather wait and verify than pay for assumptions. Good business, unproven file: I'll watch it.
